#2016. Emery would be mad to go to United - his best route to the top is at Villa. They're close to being giants and, with him as boss, they can bridge the gap to the elite: OLIVER HOLT

Published: 04:22 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:11 EDT, 3 November 2026

Unai Emery, the man of the moment, the manager whose name is on everybody’s lips, the man that others would make their king, walked into the cavernous press conference room at the Nou Camp just after 8.15pm local time on Monday evening.

This is only a league game, early in the competition but there was electricity in the room that comes with the anticipation of the collision ahead. ‘This is elite football and Barcelona is always the favourite in a competition like this,’ Emery reminded his audience, ‘but we also have a history.

‘In 1982, we won the Champions League, the so-called European Cup. Barcelona are the favourites because of the present and what they have done over the last ten years. We are constantly seeking new challenges. We want to come here tomorrow night and see how far away we are from Barcelona.’

This is Emery against a big club. Against one of the modern elite. This is Emery and his wits against Lamine Yamal and Rodri and Raphinha. This is what Jamie Carragher, one of Emery’s most vocal – and controversial - champions of recent days, would call a ‘giant’ club. The phrase ‘Mes Que Un Club’ is even written into the seats at this magnificent stadium. It is the kind of club many believe Emery is born for.

Everybody is lavishing praise upon him. A few hours earlier, at the Barcelona training complex in Sant Joan Despi, several miles west of the city, Hansi Flick, the Barca coach, waxed lyrical about Emery’s talents and said he was the reason they were expecting such a tough match in their Champions League tie here on Tuesday evening.

‘Unai Emery is one of the best coaches in Europe and the world,’ Flick said. ‘He is very successful. In the way his team plays, you can see a clear structure in defence. And in offence, they have different patterns. For me, it is amazing to see his team.

At the Barcelona training complex, Hansi Flick, the Barca coach, waxed lyrical about Emery’s talents and said he was the reason they were expecting such a tough match

Flick also praised Nicolas Jackson, the Villa striker who has found his form under Emery

‘Their start this season was not easy, but they came back. You can see the confidence they have on the ball, how they play out, and Nicolas Jackson is at an unbelievable level. For us, it will be a tough game against a good team and, as well, a great coach.’

Anthony Gordon, who joined Barcelona from Newcastle United in the summer, had already given a press conference of impressive maturity and thoughtfulness that had taken in his love of books and his distrust of TikTok but he, too, was unstinting in his admiration for Emery.

'Villa are a very good team,’ Gordon said. ‘They have one of the best coaches in the world right now. They are on a great run of late as well, so it will be a difficult game. They are one of the teams who are always in a game and are always ready for any type of game. It will be a very tough challenge.’

Even the environs of the stadium seemed to pay homage to Emery’s talents. Cranes still lean over the stands here as the extensive renovations to the steepling stands continue. Emery, we all know, is the master of the rebuild.

So by the time Emery walked out into that auditorium, it felt almost as if this were a final audition. This is the kind of stuff that, understandably, enrages Villa and their fans because of its patronising tone but the more impressive his results with his club, the more people suggest he should go elsewhere.

That is what got Carragher in trouble. Carragher said Manchester United should be making him their number one target because he is the best manager in the league. ‘Surely, he would want the opportunity to manage a giant again,’ Carragher said, aiming a couple of expletives at Villa supporters for good measure.

Villa chairman Nassef Sawiris threatened to take legal action against Carragher, Carragher apologised and all was forgotten. But while Emery thrives and a manager at one of the elite European clubs struggles, he will continue to be linked to those positions. It is the way it has always been.

And anyway, Emery would be mad to go to United if Michael Carrick leaves Old Trafford in the next few weeks. Not just because United is a basket-case of a club run by people who would not allow the manager to have anything like the level of control he enjoys at Villa, where he has smart owners who trust him and support him to the hilt.

Emery has been talked about as a successor to Michael Carrick at Manchester United

Emery knows what it can be like at so-called bigger clubs like PSG and Arsenal, when impatience runs wild and expectations are absurd and support starts to wane. His best route to the very top is at a club like Villa. Because Villa are close to being giants and, with him as boss, they can bridge the gap to the elite.

Emery lost most of his first team in the summer - Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Lucas Digne, Emiliano Martinez, Youri Tielemans, Ollie Watkins, Donyell Malen and Leon Bailey all left – but he has fashioned a new exciting side in their stead already.

Villa are unbeaten in their last five games in the Premier League, including a victory that handed Manchester City their first defeat of the season, and sit second only to PSG at the top of the nascent Champions League table, with three straight wins. Emery is burnishing his reputation as a football magician. He is the game’s hottest managerial property again.

If Villa get a result at the Nou Camp, speculation about the future of Emery, who will turn 55 on the day of the game, will run wild again. It is bound to. It is a compliment to both manager and club, although it is unlikely Villa will see it that way. The joy of the results he is producing is tempered only by the fear of losing him.

But for all his success in Europe – he has won the Europa League five times, most recently with Villa in Istanbul last summer – he has a miserable record at the Nou Camp. He has brought six different clubs here and lost 14 of the 15 matches he has managed. His sole victory was with Villarreal in May 2022.

He has one particular ghost to slay in this competition. Because the Nou Camp was the scene of La Remontada, or ‘the comeback’, when Emery’s PSG brought a 4-0 lead to Barcelona for the second leg of a Round of 16 tie. PSG had won the first leg at the Parc des Princes 4-0 in March 2017 but Barcelona swept them aside 6-1 back in Catalonia.

The mention of that game was the one time during the press conference when Emery bristled. When asked what his memory of it was, he said sharply: ‘One more.’ Just one game among hundreds, he seemed to be saying. ‘I played in Europe 16 years in a row and I have learned in all of them. I learned so, so much. That night, I learned on sports side and not the sports side.’

Alongside him, John McGinn spoke compellingly, too. He spoke about coming here just once before, on a stadium tour when he was eight years old and he and his family were on their way to a holiday in the Canary Islands.

Emery has one particular ghost to slay in this competition because the Nou Camp was the scene of La Remontada, when his PSG side lost despite coming with a 4-0 lead in the first leg

‘I am 32 years old and the trajectory of this club is allowing me to dream the dream of playing in front of the biggest crowds in the biggest arenas,’ McGinn said. ‘We want to make this a yearly experience to compete with the biggest teams in England and Europe.’

Emery also mentioned Gordon as one of the components he admires in the Barcelona side. Listening to him earlier, it was clear that he has already grown, both on and off the pitch since his move to Spanish football.

‘The challenge of joining Barca is different to what I've had before,’ Gordon said, ‘because when I was at Everton, I was fighting relegation for two or three years, which was tough. At Newcastle we were fighting for the Champions League and to push up the tables, and now I am at a club where we are fighting for every trophy.

‘I really enjoyed all three because they come with different things to help you as a person, help you grow. I think to be competing on every front for every trophy is definitely the most enjoyable. I think people think it's more pressure, but it's actually less pressure than fighting relegation and fighting to push up the table for the Champions League. I want to win every trophy. I want to be the best. This club allows me to do so.’

Before he left, Gordon spoke about how he rations his time on social media and reads more books and goes on more walks. ‘When you're in that wheel of dopamine addiction and you're scrolling on social media, you have to come away from it and get back to what’s real,’ he said.

On Tuesday night in the Nou Camp, Emery and Villa will take the next step on their advance on Europe and the rest of us will find out what is real and what is not.

#2015. Player Ratings: AC Milan 3-1 Inter – Moreira show; De Winter responds

AC Milan clinched a massive win at San Siro to paint the city of Milan red and black. Below are the player ratings for the Rossoneri, with several high ones handed out.

After an up-and-down start to the season, Milan headed into the Derby della Madonnina knowing that a win would make all the difference. Gerry Cardinale said as much before the game and luckily, they succeeded with a 3-1 win.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

If you haven’t already, make sure to check out how we decide the player ratings. From the scale to what affects the rating, we have compiled everything there.

🥇 Moreira (9.5 – MOTM): He’s rough around the edges sometimes, but with one fantastic goal and two very good assists in a derby, he deserves all the praise he can get. I expressed doubts about him playing on the right but tonight was his best game in that role. Really, really encouraging ahead of what’s to come.

👎 Everyone got over a 6 tonight, so there was no flop.

👔 Amorim (7): Individual brilliance was the difference-maker, BUT, it would be rude not to acknowledge some of Amorim’s moves tonight. He got the starting eleven spot on, waited with the substitutions, and gave his players good advice at the interval to avoid another push from Inter in the second half.

Maignan (8): He made a fantastic save on Spence in the first half, using his reflexes, and it’s a save that really paved the way for the win. There were other good interventions too, like the volleyball-esque clearance on Calhanoglu’s corner, and coming out to head the ball away. CAPITANO!

Gila (7): I don’t think it’s a coincidence that Milan suddenly looked much more solid with him back in the defensive four. That said, he didn’t stand out with any major interventions, but was just very good through calm passing, good positioning and marshalling. When he’s back to 100% fit, he will be even more important.

De Winter (8): He absolutely won the battle against Thuram this game and it’s not like it was an easy one either. The two had several 50-50 duels and he always came out on top. Aside from his Thuram battle, he was very good overall and deserves a high rating here.

Pavlovic (7.5): It was a bit of a roller coaster for him, but allow me to explain. He left Bastoni on the goal and simply shouldn’t have, for many reasons, and then he also missed a good chance in attack. However, the second half was brilliant with several last-ditch clearances/tackles, including a wonderful one on Barella to stop a goal. That tackle was worth everything in my opinion.

Diawara (6.5): Considering it was his first derby, and game of this calibre, we have to give him praise. He had a cautious style and it worked tonight, as he often just needed to stop his man/block the cross rather than trying to make something extraordinary with the ball. One good cross in attack for Pavlovic, which we shouldn’t forget.

Moreira (9.5 – MOTM): He’s rough around the edges sometimes, but with one fantastic goal and two very good assists in a derby, he deserves all the praise he can get. I expressed doubts about him playing on the right but tonight was his best game in that role. Really, really encouraging ahead of what’s to come.

Musah (7): He won the free-kick that Moreira converted with some smart body work. In addition to that, he was very composed (something he often struggles with) and really helped Milan get out of several tough/tight situations. One poor giveaway at the end but overall, very solid.

Modric (7.5): The veteran stayed on for the entire 90 minutes and fought until the very end. There was one sequence in the final minutes/last ten or so when he really had to scrap to get out of a tight jam, and did so successfully. What a player.

Pulisic (8): It was a great header to open the scoring for Milan, celebrating his renewal in style. The positioning is what makes him so brilliant, not just on the goal but also how he links the midfield and attack together. Could he have been even more effective on the ball? Yes, but the importance of the movement shouldn’t be played down just because it wasn’t always fireworks.

Rabiot (7.5): I’m stunned by the awareness to opt for a finish like that on the goal, but that’s why he’s such a highly-rated footballer. He was good aside from that but perhaps could have been even more effective on the ball for a higher rating. Then again, his movement and running is key.

Ramos (6.5): It feels like I say it every game, aside from the last one when he genuinely looked tired, but the running helps Milan so much in opening up space. Now, his rating is not super high here and that’s because he can still do more on the ball/in the box, but it was good.

Since all the substitutions were made from the 82nd minute onwards, I just didn’t see enough to give either of them a rating.

Bartesaghi, Jashari, Cisse, Terracciano and Hutchinson: N/A

Amorim (7): Individual brilliance was the difference-maker, BUT, it would be rude not to acknowledge some of Amorim’s moves tonight. He got the starting eleven spot on, waited with the substitutions, and gave his players good advice at the interval to avoid another push from Inter in the second half.

#2014. Cardiff v West Ham Preview: Parker Era Beckons After Nuno Sacking

Cardiff City v West Ham United EFL Championship Cardiff City Stadium Wednesday 4 November 2026, 7.45pm GMT

West Ham United’s crucial Championship match at Cardiff City will take place against the backdrop of a dramatic managerial change. Nuno Espírito Santo has been sacked with immediate effect following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion.

Scott Parker is expected to replace him, with discussions at an advanced stage and an official announcement anticipated. However, at the time of writing, West Ham have only confirmed that Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville are preparing the squad for Wednesday night.

The change completely transforms the complexion of a match which had looked capable of determining Nuno’s future. West Ham now travel to Wales looking for an immediate response, a much-needed lift and the first glimpse of what could become Parker’s latest Championship promotion challenge.

Scott Parker knows how to get out of the Championship

West Ham confirmed Nuno’s departure following what the club described as a thorough review of the Championship season. Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left, bringing the Portuguese coach’s reign to a complete end.

The decision is hardly surprising after Saturday’s dreadful 3-1 defeat against West Brom. West Ham showed little motivation, lacked a coherent tactical plan and were repeatedly exposed by a team operating with far greater organisation and purpose.

Nuno leaves the Hammers eighth in the Championship after six victories from 13 league matches. We are six points behind leaders Middlesbrough and four away from the automatic-promotion places, which is not an insurmountable position but is considerably worse than expected.

The official statement explained that the board believed change was necessary to keep the club’s objectives on track. That is difficult to argue with because West Ham’s target was never to scrape into the play-offs; it was to secure an immediate return to the Premier League.

The full announcement confirming Nuno’s departure can be read in West Ham United’s official club statement.

Scott Parker is now expected to become West Ham’s new head coach. The former Hammer has been identified as the leading candidate, with multiple reports suggesting an agreement has been reached and only the formal announcement remains outstanding.

Parker’s record in the Championship is the obvious attraction. He has won promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley, meaning he understands both the division and the specific challenge West Ham face.

He also knows the club. Parker made 129 appearances for the Hammers between 2007 and 2011, captained the team and won Hammer of the Year in three consecutive seasons.

According to our latest information, Parker’s proposed contract is heavily linked to promotion. He is expected to receive a longer-term opportunity if he takes West Ham up, while the club would retain protection if that objective is not achieved.

The timing creates an unusual situation before Wednesday’s match. West Ham have stated that Noble, Potts and Prenderville are temporarily overseeing preparations, but Parker could still be formally appointed before the squad travels to Wales.

Whether he would immediately take charge from the dugout remains unclear. Even if he does, there will be very little time for Parker to introduce significant tactical changes or properly assess a squad he has not coached.

That means the team will probably have to rely upon a reaction to Nuno’s departure rather than any sophisticated new system. The players can no longer hide behind complaints about the previous manager’s tactics, selections or motivational skills.

This is now an opportunity for them to demonstrate that they are considerably better than recent performances have suggested.

Changing the manager does not automatically correct everything which went wrong against Southampton and West Brom. West Ham remain vulnerable defensively, disjointed in midfield and overly reliant upon Jarrod Bowen in attack.

My preferred formation remains a 4-1-4-1, accompanied by drastic changes. Alphonse Areola deserves an opportunity in goal because Mads Hermansen has not done enough to make himself untouchable.

Joël Veltman should start at right-back, with Airidas Golambeckis partnering Max Kilman if Dinos Mavropanos remains unavailable. Kyle Walker-Peters would play on the left if he recovers from the injury sustained against West Brom, although his fitness remains uncertain.

Soungoutou Magassa should operate as the holding midfielder, providing the defensive protection West Ham have been missing. Lewis Orford and Divine Mukasa would then be free to play ahead of him, rather than being asked to perform roles which do not suit their strengths.

Edvin Austbø and Bowen would provide the width, with Joël Piroe finally receiving a proper opportunity as the central striker. As I argued before Nuno’s dismissal, West Ham need to stop repeating the same selection mistakes.

The managerial upheaval makes an honest predicted XI almost impossible. This is therefore the team I would hand to Parker or the interim coaching staff, subject to Walker-Peters and Mavropanos being declared fit.

Cardiff sit 17th after gaining promotion as League One runners-up last season. Brian Barry-Murphy’s team had been unbeaten in three before suffering a 3-0 defeat at Wolverhampton Wanderers on Saturday.

The Bluebirds could also have up to eight players unavailable. Gabriel Osho is suspended, while Will Fish, Perry Ng, Dylan Lawlor, Calum Chambers, Krystian Bielik, Alex Robertson and Isaak Davies are injury doubts.

That does not guarantee West Ham anything, particularly during a turbulent 24 hours at the club. However, it gives the Hammers a very good opportunity to respond immediately and begin repairing the damage caused by consecutive defeats.

The mood around the squad should already have changed. Players who were overlooked or used incorrectly by Nuno now have the chance to impress a new coaching team, while those who had become automatic selections can no longer take their places for granted.

My original prediction was a 1-1 draw, largely because nothing about West Ham’s recent performances inspired confidence. Nuno’s dismissal introduces the possibility of a reaction, but it does not instantly repair the team’s defensive and attacking problems.

West Ham possess more than enough ability to beat a depleted Cardiff team. The uncertainty is whether the players can produce a coherent performance so soon after a major managerial change.

I expect greater energy and urgency, but I will retain my original prediction until we know whether Parker will be in the dugout and which players are available.

Prediction: Cardiff City 1-1 West Ham United

#2013. Tactical change could revitalise Arne Engels if Nuno is ready to grasp the nettle | West Ham News

Arne Engels needs to be freed from the defensive duties with which he’s weighed down by West Ham’s current formation.

At least, that’s the gist of a report published last night suggesting that the Hammers need an old fashioned defensive midfielder at the heart of their side, to block off teams who at present appear to be able to play through their non-existent defensive shield owing to both Engels and Mukasa venturing too far forward too often.

As the 4thofficial suggested, there’s a remedy already at hand, a player largely ignored by Nuno yet one who could possibly could have a role to play in a more defensively solid West Ham United team, which is, frankly desperate to stop the early goals going in: Recalling defensive midfielder Edson Alvarez.

“From West Ham‘s perspective, reinstating Álvarez should come before abandoning the entire tactical framework. Engels has potential, but expecting the Belgian to provide attacking quality and defensive protection simultaneously places unnecessary pressure on an inexperienced midfield partnership.

Álvarez could give the centre-backs greater protection when attacking full-backs advance, while allowing Engels more freedom to distribute and move forward. That adjustment would address an immediate weakness without forcing another expensive recruitment exercise.”

Many have written off Alvarez as being too slow or too volatile in view of his disciplinary record – which other than an infamous red card against Liverpool – is perhaps not as bad as projected.

Report suggests the scrap- heap midfielder could do a job for Nuno.. if the West Ham manager is  big enough to mend bridges with El Machin

Many Claret and Hugh readers have commented that Nuno’s side needs the extra solidity of a ‘number six’ sitting in front of the back line to which, in truth, Engels doesn’t seem to be best suited.

Perhaps, indeed, rather than abandon the whole ‘tactical framework’ or trying to fit yet another square peg into a round hole, Nuno could grasp the nettle and re-integrate the tailor made defensive minded midfielder Alvarez into his line up.

There’s a down side of course. Dropping one of Mukasa or Kanté  would reduce West Ham’s creativity going forward. It could mean reverting Kanté to the bench blunderbuss role for the second half of games, exactly as he started the season so successfully.

It might make the Irons harder to score against in the first ’45 minutes anyway, Which at the moment couldn’t be such a bad thing. Is Nuno ready to grasp the nettle? Something has to give because right now, ‘hard work’ and ‘talking about it‘ isn’t fixing anything.

#2011. Three Defeats And Gone: What Křetínský’s History Means For Nuno

West Ham supporters wondering how long Daniel Křetínský will continue backing Nuno Espírito Santo might find some surprising answers in the Czech billionaire’s history at Sparta Prague. Because while the Hammers manager currently appears secure in his position, Křetínský has previously been involved in managerial decisions that make Nuno’s recent difficulties look relatively modest.

In one particularly extraordinary example, Sparta dismissed a manager despite being nine points clear at the top of the league. Another departed following three damaging defeats in quick succession.

And having looked into Křetínský’s history, I’m beginning to wonder whether Nuno’s position at West Ham is quite as secure as many of us have assumed.

Kretinsky has a history of being ruthless with underperforming coaches

Křetínský became involved in Sparta Prague’s ownership and management in 2004, when investment group J&T acquired the club. He subsequently became chairman and has overseen an extraordinary number of managerial changes.

Perhaps the most remarkable came in December 2004, when František Straka was dismissed despite Sparta being nine points clear at the top of the Czech league.

Yes, you read that correctly. Nine points clear.

Even more interestingly, Křetínský explained the decision himself in an October 2008 interview with Czech newspaper iDNES.

The club’s sporting leadership had lost confidence in Straka’s footballing system. With Champions League qualification looking secure, Křetínský decided to make the change early to give a replacement time to prepare.

He subsequently admitted the decision was a mistake.

Nevertheless, it provides an extraordinary insight into his thinking. League position alone was not enough to protect a manager if Křetínský lacked confidence in his methods.

The example I found particularly interesting was Vítězslav Lavička, whose first spell as Sparta manager lasted just 123 days in 2008.

Lavička had started reasonably well, but three damaging defeats in quick succession changed everything.

Sparta lost 3-0 against Slovan Liberec, suffered European elimination against Dinamo Zagreb and were then thrashed 4-1 by Slavia Prague.

Lavička subsequently left the club, with the departing coach explaining that he had rejected conditions attached to his continued employment.

So this wasn’t quite a straightforward dismissal. Nevertheless, three damaging results had helped bring a very short managerial reign to an abrupt end.

Considering West Ham have just suffered consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, I find that particularly interesting.

In February 2021, Sparta dismissed Václav Kotal despite the club sitting second in the Czech league.

In Sparta’s official announcement, sporting director Tomáš Rosický explained that management believed the team’s objectives were under threat and performances were deteriorating.

In other words, second place wasn’t considered sufficient protection when the club believed things were heading in the wrong direction.

Similarly, when Lavička returned for a second spell, he was dismissed in April 2015 with Sparta five points behind the league leaders and several seasonal objectives already missed.

These later decisions were made within Sparta’s wider management structure, so it would be wrong to suggest Křetínský personally ordered every dismissal.

A loss against Cardiff could spell danger for Nuno

Until now, I’ve been fairly convinced that Nuno is extremely secure in his job.

After all, it was Křetínský who backed the manager during the summer despite David Sullivan apparently wanting a change.

My assumption was that having made such a significant decision, the Czech billionaire would be reluctant to admit he had backed the wrong man.

Having researched his Sparta Prague history, I’m no longer so sure.

There is nothing in that record to suggest Křetínský will necessarily stick with a manager simply because he appointed or supported him.

If anything, what he has consistently demonstrated is a willingness to sanction managerial change when his club’s principal objectives appear to be slipping away.

At Sparta, that generally meant winning titles or securing European qualification.

At West Ham, the equivalent objective is automatic promotion back to the Premier League.

And having dropped to eighth in the Championship, following another dreadful home defeat, Nuno certainly isn’t making that task look particularly straightforward.

Of course, Sparta Prague and West Ham have different ownership structures, and none of this proves Křetínský is currently considering dismissing Espírito Santo.

But it has changed my assessment of the situation.

I no longer believe Nuno can necessarily survive a sustained period outside the automatic promotion places.

And if Křetínský’s history tells us anything, it’s that backing a manager today offers no guarantee he’ll still be backing him tomorrow.

#2010. West Ham Sack Nuno As Křetínský Loses Patience

West Ham United have confirmed that Nuno Espírito Santo has been sacked with immediate effect following mounting pressure on the Hammers head coach over the past few days.

The Portuguese manager’s position had become increasingly precarious following consecutive defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, with concerns growing behind the scenes that the club’s automatic promotion ambitions were slipping away.

As Claret & Hugh reported earlier, there had been growing indications from within the club that Nuno was no longer safe in his position. Daniel Křetínský was understood to be increasingly unimpressed with performances, and the decision to act suggests the West Ham hierarchy were no longer prepared to allow the situation to continue.

Rumours had also emerged yesterday that discussions were already taking place over the identity of West Ham’s next head coach, suggesting that preparations for a possible managerial change were underway.

The decision is particularly significant given Křetínský’s previous backing of Nuno. However, as our earlier research into his managerial decisions at Sparta Prague demonstrated, the Czech billionaire has a history of making changes when he believes a club’s objectives are under threat.

West Ham have now confirmed that the change has been made following a review of the Championship campaign.

In an official statement, the club announced:

West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team Head Coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the Board of Directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the Club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.

Assistant Head Coach Rui Pedro Silva and Goalkeeper Coach Rui Barbosa have also departed.

West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the Club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

The process of recruiting a new Head Coach is already underway.

Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of squad preparations ahead of tomorrow evening’s EFL Championship fixture at Cardiff City, and the Club will make no further comment until the appointment of the new Head Coach is confirmed.

West Ham must now move quickly to appoint a replacement, with the Championship promotion race continuing and tomorrow night’s trip to Cardiff City fast approaching.

#2009. Asia Cup is POSTPONED just two months before its start due to safety concerns in Saudi Arabia - in huge boost to Premier League clubs

Published: 03:25 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:13 EDT, 3 November 2026

The 2027 Asia Cup has been delayed by almost a year amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Less than two months before it was due to kick off, the tournament hosted by Saudi Arabia has been postponed until December 2027 after the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict re-escalated.

Major airports in Saudi Arabia are operating reduced services after a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people. Two people were also killed after an attack at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

It makes the tournament not only a logistical nightmare for the 24 participating teams but also raises serious safety concerns.

A statement from the Asian Football Confederation said: 'The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved rescheduling the flagship national team tournament considering the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions.

'The new dates of the tournament (December 23 2027 to January 21 2028) will be presented to FIFA for approval.

'Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the Competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.'

However, the delay boosts several Premier League clubs, who no longer face losing players for up to a month of the season. Japan had ten Premier League players available for selection, with Aston Villa potentially losing first-choice goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

Aston Villa could have been without Zion Suzuki, who has kept three clean sheets this season, for five Premier League matches and their last two league phase matches in the Champions League

Japan international Daichi Kamada has started all nine of Crystal Palace's Premier League matches this season

Crystal Palace could have been without Takehiro Tomiyasu and Daichi Kamada for up to five Premier League matches had Japan reached the final.

Ipswich's Daizen Maeda, who has made ten appearances this season, was likely to be called up alongside Brighton's Kaoru Mitoma, who is currently sidelined.

Manchester City, meanwhile, were expected to lose Uzbek international Abdukodir Khusanov.

This is the second successive tournament to be postponed after the 2023 edition was delayed by a year due to the Covid pandemic.

The Asia Cup is not the first event in Saudi Arabia to be disrupted after the PIF-backed Asian Tour Saudi International golf tournament was indefinitely postponed.

Meanwhile, the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament - featuring Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev - in Riyadh has been cancelled.

It is not a complete whitewash, though. Last weekend, Canelo Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title, beating Christian Mbilli on points in Riyadh. Riyadh will also play host to WWE Crown Jewel on Saturday.

The Formula 1 season concludes in the Middle East, with the penultimate race taking place in Qatar at the end of the month, followed by the season finale in Abu Dhabi at the start of December.

F1 intends to go ahead with both races but is continuing to monitor the situation.

Meanwhile, the second race of next season is scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia in mid-March. There are currently no plans to cancel the event, despite this year's race having been called off.

#2008. West Ham Exclusive: Scott Parker Emerges As Leading Candidate

Claret & Hugh can reveal this morning that West Ham United have already held discussions with a number of potential replacements for Nuno Espírito Santo, who was dismissed with immediate effect earlier today.

Some of those meetings took place as recently as yesterday, although the club have been describing the discussions as a sounding-out process rather than formal interviews.

Nevertheless, it appears the decision to part company with Nuno was effectively made following Saturday’s 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion, with the Hammers hierarchy already exploring their options before this morning’s announcement.

#2007. West Ham Insider Reveals Nuno’s Striker Gamble Before Sacking

Following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo, questions are inevitably being asked about what went wrong during his time at West Ham United. And while there are plenty of areas worth examining, one of the most revealing concerns the Hammers’ striking department.

As Claret & Hugh learned from a West Ham insider before Nuno’s departure, the club’s three recognised centre-forwards were all specifically wanted by the Portuguese coach. That information is particularly significant given the team’s struggles in front of goal and the manager’s apparent reluctance to use some of the players he recruited.

The source’s assessment was straightforward: “They were all Nuno’s picks.”

It is a revelation that makes some of the decisions taken during the Championship campaign even harder to understand, particularly now that the manager has paid the price for West Ham’s disappointing performances.

The transfers attributed to recruitment director Nils Koppen have enjoyed varying degrees of success, and I still believe the jury is out on whether West Ham overpaid for Arne Engels.

But as Koppen himself explained, he had a very short period of time at the London Stadium before the summer transfer window closed.

What is not in doubt, according to our source, is that Nuno wanted Taty Castellanos, Pablo and Joël Piroe.

And it is the situation surrounding Piroe that I find particularly interesting.

“Nuno pushed really hard for Piroe because of his Championship goalscoring record. I’m surprised he hasn’t played more.”

Nuno pushed hard for Piroe but didn’t play him

Piroe arrived with a proven record of scoring goals in the Championship, something West Ham desperately needed following relegation.

Yet despite the Hammers’ continuing struggles in front of goal, he was given relatively limited opportunities to establish himself.

If Nuno was so determined to sign him, why was he so reluctant to play him?

It’s a perfectly reasonable question, particularly when neither Castellanos nor Pablo has done enough to make himself indispensable.

As we have already highlighted, the constant chopping and changing in attack did little to help any of West Ham’s forwards find form.

And if all three were Nuno’s preferred signings, it becomes considerably harder to blame the recruitment department for the lack of goals.

There had also been growing concern behind the scenes at the London Stadium that Espírito Santo did not know his best team.

It was a criticism supporters had been making for some time, and one that became increasingly difficult to dismiss as the manager continued changing personnel and formations.

The defeat against West Bromwich Albion provided another example of a team struggling for cohesion, creativity and confidence.

Ordinarily, in times gone by at West Ham, a certain amount of player frustration would eventually find its way back to David Sullivan.

Whether that happened in this instance remains unclear, particularly given the uncertainty surrounding the club’s ownership and decision-making structure.

But irrespective of any input from players, it had become increasingly evident that concerns were growing within the Hammers hierarchy.

The subsequent decision to dismiss Nuno confirms that the board believed a change was necessary, although it does not establish which individual concerns proved decisive.

Of course, Nuno’s departure doesn’t magically solve West Ham’s goalscoring problems.

Castellanos, Pablo and Piroe remain at the club, and whoever takes over will have to find a way of getting considerably more from them.

But that is also what makes the appointment of a new manager so interesting.

We have spent months wondering whether the problem was the players themselves or the way they were being used.

Now somebody else will have an opportunity to find out.

And perhaps the most revealing test will be what happens to Piroe, the proven Championship goalscorer whom Nuno apparently wanted so badly but seemed so reluctant to select.

#2006. Cardinale emotional after Milan derby win: “It makes me want to cry”

Gerry Cardinale could not hide his delight after AC Milan beat city rivals Inter to win the derby 3-1 on Saturday night.

It was a memorable night for Milan at San Siro as they claimed the bragging rights for the fourth time in a row with a commanding win. Christian Pulisic, Adrien Rabiot and Diego Moreira all scored in the first half to put the Rossoneri on course, and they would see out the win from there.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

#2005. “Welcome Back” Paco On The Market Following Dismissal | West Ham News

Former West Ham assistant coach Paco Jémez is once again searching for a new club after being relieved of his duties by Moroccan giants Raja Casablanca following a disappointing start to the season.

Jémez earned admirers for the attacking brand of football he implemented in Spain, and many supporters pointed to the turnaround in performances at West Ham as being credited to him.

However, his latest managerial venture has come to an abrupt end after Raja Casablanca opted to make a change just over two months after appointing him.

The club confirmed that Sunday’s 2-0 defeat to RS Berkane would be Jémez’s final match in charge, with officials deciding a fresh approach was needed after reviewing the team’s performances and results.

An official club statement explained that the sporting management felt a change in technical leadership was necessary to provide a new dynamic and improve the club’s chances of meeting its objectives this season.

Despite arriving in Casablanca with an impressive CV that included spells at Rayo Vallecano, Granada, Las Palmas and Mexican side Cruz Azul, the Spaniard struggled to generate momentum. Raja collected just six points from their opening five league fixtures, winning once, drawing three times and losing once.

Those results left his new club down in 13th place and under growing pressure, a situation made worse by a run of performances that failed to convince supporters.

Reports in Morocco had suggested Jémez’s future was already under scrutiny before the defeat against Berkane, with the coach reportedly asking club officials for more time to improve results. However, the latest setback proved decisive.

Following the defeat, Jémez accepted responsibility and apologised to supporters, acknowledging that the team had not produced the level of performance expected from one of Morocco’s biggest clubs. He also stated that he would accept whatever decision the board deemed appropriate.

West Ham ultimately went in a different direction by appointing Rui Pedro Silva as assistant head coach in the summer, despite Jémez publicly stating he wanted to stay on. Yet as of this morning, things have moved on!

Jémez’s latest dismissal serves as a reminder of the ruthless nature of football management.

A coach once regarded as one of Spain’s most innovative tacticians now finds himself looking for a fresh opportunity after another short-lived spell in the dugout.

#2004. Lewis Ferguson insists Rangers move 'will happen' in big transfer declaration

Lewis Ferguson has revealed he expects to play for Rangers one day as the Scotland star opened up on his future.

The Bologna captain has established himself as one of the leading Scottish players abroad after moving to Italy in 2022, with his performances regularly prompting speculation over what could come next.

But the former Aberdeen midfielder has admitted a move to Ibrox is something he believes will eventually happen.

Asked about the prospect of following in the footsteps of his father and uncle, both former Rangers players, Ferguson said: “Ah, I know... Rangers? Let’s just say that sooner or later, I’ll go there; one day I know it’ll happen. [Gazzetta]

"The rest is about today: we’ve bounced back now, and we have to ride this wave.”

For now, though, Ferguson remains firmly committed to Bologna. The Scotland international revealed he received interest over the summer but ultimately decided to remain in Italy after reflecting on everything the club had given him.

45-cap Rangers star left out for Scotland clash as national boss reveals reason

Rangers learn match officials for Saturday night Premiership clash vs St Mirren

Rangers hero 'set' for new role at EFL side after leaving last club over summer

He explained: “I’d taken a bit of time out. I’d had some enquiries, yes, but I wanted to figure out exactly what to do with my life, whether to change direction or carry on as I was.

“Then I thought: Bologna has given me so much. On top of that, the Champions League, the Coppa Italia won and lifted as captain, the Europa League which... if we hadn’t come up against Aston Villa, we’d have reached the final, then the moments of friendship, even the tough times like the injury.

“In short: I took my time and then said just four words: Bologna is my home. And I want to stay here for at least another year.”

Ferguson later reiterated his affection for the Italian club while refusing to put a definitive timescale on his stay. He added: “I’m certainly not thinking about how long I’ll stay, but I’m definitely thinking about how I’ll stay.

"Bologna has been home since day one, I’ll say it again, and I’m having a brilliant time here.”

The midfielder has also embraced the responsibility of captaining Bologna, an achievement he described as a major source of pride as a Scotsman playing abroad.

#2003. West Ham Exclusive: Parker’s Promotion Clause And Nuno’s £3m Payoff Revealed

Scott Parker is expected to sign a two-and-a-half-year contract with West Ham United this afternoon, with Claret & Hugh receiving fresh information about the proposed deal and the compensation package for departing manager Nuno Espírito Santo.

A club insider briefed C&H within the last few moments, revealing that Parker’s agreement includes break clauses linked directly to whether West Ham secure promotion back to the Premier League at the first attempt. We have also been informed that Nuno is set to receive just under £3million in compensation following his dismissal this morning.

The details represent a significant development following our earlier exclusive identifying Parker as the leading candidate to replace the Portuguese coach. The former Hammers midfielder now appears close to completing his return to the London Stadium, although the appointment has yet to be officially announced.

It will coast West Ham just under £3m to sack Rui Pedro Silva & Nuno Espirito Santo

According to our source, Parker has been more than happy to accept the proposed terms, with a genuine desire within the club to see him succeed.

Speaking to Claret & Hugh within the last few moments, the insider explained:

“Parker will need to get West Ham up this season. If he doesn’t, he’ll be released without compensation. If he gets promoted to the Premier League, it will activate a two-year deal.”

In effect, Parker’s longer-term future at West Ham will depend upon achieving promotion this season.

Failure to return to the Premier League would allow the club to part company with the manager without paying compensation, according to the information we have received.

Promotion, however, would activate the remaining two years of his contract.

Claret & Hugh have also been informed that Parker will be given the opportunity to manage West Ham in the Premier League should he secure promotion.

That assurance is particularly interesting given his dismissal by Burnley last season, despite having previously guided the Clarets into the top flight.

Parker’s experience of winning promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley appears to have been a significant factor in West Ham’s interest.

The Hammers hierarchy are evidently prioritising a manager with a proven Championship promotion record, while protecting the club financially should their objectives not be achieved.

Meanwhile, Nuno’s departure, confirmed earlier this morning, is expected to cost West Ham just short of £3million in compensation.

The proposed agreement with Parker would therefore represent a very different financial arrangement, with the club’s promotion ambitions written directly into the terms of his employment.

An official announcement confirming Parker’s appointment is still awaited.

#2002. Newcastle United young stars with brilliant win over League Two side to progress for first time in 8 years

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A great Tuesday night for the Newcastle United young stars as they beat the Rotherham United first team 1-0 at the New York Stadium.

Now renamed the Jersey Mike’s Trophy, the EFL Trophy is a cup competition for all League One and League Two clubs, plus under 21 sides from 16 Category One Academies (Arsenal, Aston Villa, Brentford, Brighton & Hove Albion, Chelsea, Crystal Palace, Everton, Fulham, Ipswich Town, Leeds United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Newcastle United, Nottingham Forest, Sunderland and Tottenham Hotspur).

After an excellent 3-1 win away (the League One and Two clubs always have home advantage) at League Two club York City and an unlucky 2-1 defeat away at League One Bradford City, the Newcastle United young stars had to beat League Two Rotherham United to ensure progress from Northern Group C.

It was 17-year-old Kyran Thompson (pictured at the top of this report) who was the match winner, a very clever finish in the 34th minute to round off an excellent team move involving Alfie Seldon and Vakhtang Salia.

Thompson chose to move from Arsenal to Newcastle United this summer and looks a real star in the making.

It was a real team effort though and a very youthful NUFC Under 21 side controlled the game, 16-year-old keeper Roman Dowell made a few saves in the first half but didn’t face a single shot on target after the break.

As well as the winning goal from Kyran Thompson, the Newcastle United young stars went close with a header from Miodrag Pivas. Michael Mills saw a free-kick well saved and the home keeper also prevented Kyran Thompson scoring his second goal.

Rotherham United are currently managed by Alex Bruce, son of our old mate Steve.

This 1-0 victory makes it five wins in a row in league and cup for the Newcastle United Under 21s.

It also means a first time in eight years that the Newcastle United young stars have progressed to the last 32 of the EFL Trophy.

That came in the 2018-19 season and ended up with the hilarious last 16 match where the Sunderland first team had the humiliation of having to play the Newcastle United kids in a competitive match. The Mackems won that game and progressed all the way to Wembley in what was then known as the Checkatrade Trophy, only to lose to Portsmouth in the final.

Newcastle (3-4-3): Roman Dowell; Henry Johnson, Miodrag Pivas, Logan Watts; Matheos Ferreira (Luke Craggs 74), Scott Bailey, Mason Miley (Jayden Kouossu 74), Dylan Charlton; Kyran Thompson (Guy Bloomer 90), Vakhtang Salia (Michael Mills 74), Alfie Seldon (Kyle Fitzgerald 74)

#2001. Ruthless Křetínský Refuses To Gamble His West Ham Reputation On Nuno Any Longer

Daniel Křetínský has demonstrated that there is a limit to how far he is prepared to gamble his reputation at West Ham United on Nuno Espírito Santo. Having backed the Portuguese coach during the summer, the Czech billionaire has now seen the club abandon that decision following a disappointing start to the Championship campaign.

It represents a significant change of direction for West Ham, particularly given the circumstances surrounding Nuno’s retention after relegation. David Sullivan had reportedly favoured a managerial change, but Křetínský supported the idea of continuity and giving the existing head coach an opportunity to lead the promotion campaign.

At the time, I could understand the argument, even if I wasn’t convinced by it. But following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, West Ham’s board has now decided that the situation cannot continue.

There was always an element of risk attached to retaining Nuno following relegation.

He had failed to keep West Ham in the Premier League, but the argument for keeping him was that he knew the squad, understood the club and could provide the stability needed for an immediate return.

Unfortunately, that stability never really materialised.

West Ham have spent much of the Championship campaign struggling to establish a recognisable playing style, with the manager regularly changing formations and personnel.

And despite the considerable talent available to him, Nuno appeared increasingly unable to get the best out of his players.

The 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion was particularly damaging because it exposed so many of the problems supporters had been highlighting for months.

The team looked disorganised, short of confidence and heavily reliant on Jarrod Bowen to produce something out of nothing.

It was hardly the performance of a side looking capable of securing automatic promotion.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer

The decision to retain Nuno was never simply about the manager.

West Ham had already committed themselves to a huge financial gamble following relegation, selling a substantial amount of their most valuable talent while attempting to rebuild a squad capable of returning to the Premier League.

There was an understandable desire to reduce costs, but also an expectation that the club would use its remaining resources wisely.

And that is where Nuno’s continued struggles became particularly worrying.

Having sold so much of the family silver during the summer, West Ham cannot simply assume they will get another opportunity to flex their financial muscle in the Championship.

A second season outside the Premier League could present an entirely different challenge.

The club needs good coaching, sensible recruitment and a clear tactical identity.

As Nils Koppen’s plans for a recognisable West Ham footballing identity demonstrated, there is already an ambition to establish something more sustainable.

But that was becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the football being produced under Nuno.

What I found particularly interesting when researching Křetínský’s history at Sparta Prague was his willingness to change managers when a club’s objectives appeared to be under threat.

At Sparta, those objectives generally involved winning titles or securing Champions League football.

At West Ham, the immediate equivalent is automatic promotion.

I had previously assumed that because Křetínský backed Nuno during the summer, he would be reluctant to abandon that decision.

His Sparta record made me reconsider that assumption.

Of course, we should distinguish the board’s collective decision from any suggestion that Křetínský personally ordered Nuno’s dismissal. The club has not publicly established who drove the final decision.

Nevertheless, the outcome is clear. The manager Křetínský reportedly wanted to retain is no longer in charge.

Křetínský’s reputation will not ultimately be judged on whether he supported Nuno for a few months too long.

It will be judged on whether West Ham can get back into the Premier League.

And having taken the decision to change managers, the board now has to ensure the next appointment gives the club the best possible opportunity to achieve that objective.

There is still plenty of talent in this squad, and I remain convinced a better-organised team could produce considerably more convincing performances.

West Ham have made their decision. Now they need to make sure it was worth making.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2000. I said the priority should have been to sit Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes down…

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Back on 17 August 2026, six days before the 2026-27 Premier League season kicked off, I put an article (‘The priority should have been to sit Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes down’) up on The Mag.

I detailed how Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes were the key figures of the past five years. The manager and (eventual) captain leading Newcastle United to what had felt unimagined riches in the decade and a half before the October 2021 takeover.

Eddie Howe at the top of the tree managing his squad, with Bruno Guimaraes the talisman delivering on and off the pitch.

The second half of the 2021-22 Premier League season saw only Liverpool and Manchester City pick up more points than Newcastle United, incredible stuff by Eddie Howe and whilst Bruno Guimaraes was given time by the manager to settle in, once he scored that stunning backheel winner in his first ever start (at Southampton), Bruno never looked back.

The rest as they say is history. The four full seasons saw Bruno Guimaraes and Eddie Howe lead Newcastle United to three top seven finishes, two cup finals, two Champions League qualifications, two top five finishes, a trophy.

The 2025/26 season was a tough one, reaching the last 16 of the Champions League, the semi-finals of the Carabao, fifth round of the FA Cup, but also finishing 12th in the Premier League. Bruno Guimaraes also suffered his first injury of any magnitude when at NUFC, missing a key couple of months from February into April. I think 58 matches for such a small squad and so few real quality players was a real killer, it was mission impossible in reality in my eyes.

Back on 17 August 2026 I stated: ‘If Newcastle United fans thought that the final stages of the 2025-26 season were disappointing, fair to say that what has followed is far worse. For me it is anyway. This summer was always going to be a tough one, especially due to the UEFA SCR impact that very much limited the financial flex Newcastle United would have. Careful management of transfers in and out as well as the wage bill. The 2026-27 season was for sure going to be seriously challenging come what may.’

Now it is two and a half months after I wrote that and fair to say this season is now looking VERY seriously challenging.

Six days before this season starting, I said that because of all those challenges that our club faced, it was: ‘Something that for me meant the huge priority, the absolute priority, should have been for those in charge at Newcastle United, owners and senior staff, to sit both Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes down together and ask them what it would take for both of them to be totally committed and confident of tackling the 2026/27 season together. Our leaders staying and leading the way. That clearly didn’t happen.’

Back on 17 August 2026 I stated the obvious, well what to me felt obvious anyway: ‘I think that quite clearly Ross Wilson had been given far more power. Not a case of Eddie Howe losing all control but clearly a major shift in how the transfer window would be conducted. My belief is that Eddie Howe ended up with far less say when it came to whether players were sold and at the same time less say on which signings should be made. I think he would have still been able to say no to a signing and not have any forced on him, but Ross Wilson becoming the main man running the recruitment show.’

Back on 17 August 2026 I said my belief on what happened behind the scenes was as follows: ‘I think Kieran Trippier leaving was the first big blow. My belief is that Eddie Howe would certainly have been in favour of trying to keep him for at least one more season but the change in how things were done, meant that in my opinion, the club wouldn’t have offered Trippier the same wages and no surprise he walked away for first team football and a two year contract at Wolves. Anthony Gordon was clearly put up for sale long before last season ended and who knows what Eddie Howe thought about that. I think maybe he was accepting that one of his key players had to be sold to satisfy the UEFA SCR situation. The end of May and the end of the season, Bruno Guimaraes heads off to link up with Brazil whilst Eddie Howe takes a well deserved break. Only a couple of weeks later though and the Sandro Tonali to Tottenham claims began.’

Back on 17 August 2026 my view was: ‘I think now that when this all started in mid-June the writing was on the wall for the Newcastle United manager and captain. I believe that with Eddie Howe still in charge and Bruno and Tonali in tandem in the midfield, Newcastle United could have successfully negotiated the 2026-27 season. What exactly would have counted as success is another thing…but to me it would have been relative success that could have been achieved and that now looks a very tough ask with how things have ended up. With the Trippier and Gordon dominoes having already toppled, once Tonali followed…I think Bruno Guimaraes and Eddie Howe were all but guaranteed to fall as well.’

I went on to say in that piece six days before the NUFC 2026-27 kicking off: ‘I don’t think there is anything wrong with the targeting of young promising players as a key part of the Newcastle United plan, indeed that is what Eddie Howe proved so brilliant at, when recruiting the likes of Hall, Isak, Bruno, Gordon, Livramento, Tonali…However, this summer has seen the recruitment even younger than most of those successes under Howe and far greater risks with far less experience behind them, far more likely to fail and far more likely to take longer to reach their full potential. Newcastle United have shifted to a model that sees the Sporting Director far more pivotal in directing the transfer strategy and just maybe it might prove successful against the odds. However, I do think that for especially this coming season it has put Newcastle United at great risk.’

I take no pleasure in saying it but ‘great risk’ is very much how this now feels for Newcastle United.

I understand people debating whether or not Matthias Jaissle is the right man for Newcastle United but what is without doubt, he was handed a very difficult situation, some would say near impossible. That is, impossible to achieve in the short to medium term anything approaching what Eddie Howe did.

Back on 17 August 2026 I stated (and still believe): ‘If there had been a big sit down with Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes in May, maybe things would have been different, maybe nothing would have been different. At the same time though I think without the pair of them being at the heart of the plan going forward, it massively helped ensure they would both leave. Eddie Howe came back in early July ahead of pre-season and informed the club he would be leaving, volunteering to hold the fort until a replacement was ready to come in. Which turned out to be Matthias Jaissle.’

Speaking of things I still believe to be true.

On 17 August 2026 I said: ‘I don’t buy into this attempt to make out Bruno Guimaraes to be the big bad guy of this summer. I still don’t know what he has done wrong apart from inform the club he wanted to leave? Everything else is smoke and mirrors with talk of a super agent brought in to help get a move and so on. By the same token the Newcastle United hierarchy were clearly quite happy to move out Trippier, Gordon and Tonali for financial reasons, so Bruno Guimaraes can hardly be blamed in my opinion, when he chooses to follow them out as well. The idea that the NUFC owners and senior staff thought that moving these key players out would then still see both Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes up for staying, is straining credibility. The Newcastle United owners believing that, is on a par with when we had the farce of Alexander Isak going on strike throughout summer 2025 and the NUFC owners doing nothing to sort it. Then believing they could turn up at the very end of the window, go round his house and suddenly convince him to change his mind!!’

My article on 17 August 2026 ended with: ‘I hope for the best this coming season but fear the worst. If the worst does happen, I certainly won’t be pointing the finger at Eddie Howe and Bruno Guimaraes if it all goes pear-shaped. The Newcastle United owners have to step up belatedly and produce a cohesive long-term strategy to properly progress the club. If they don’t do that, we will have a lot more to worry about than what happens this coming season.’

Writing this now on 4 November 2026, not a great deal has changed for me.

I am still not pointing the finger of blame at Eddie Howe or Bruno Guimaraes.

My opinion is that the Newcastle United owners wrecked summer 2025 after Eddie Howe had just delivered the most successful NUFC season in living memory for most of us. A huge dereliction of duty in having no actively working Sporting Director or CEO in place, leaving Eddie Howe totally unsupported and no senior staff in place to help ensure the key Howe transfer targets were delivered. The NUFC owners insisting they wouldn’t sell Alexander Isak and then at the very last minute doing a u-turn and the rushed end of window recruitment of Woltemade and Wissa (rather than the likes of Joao Pedro and Hugo Ekitike who Howe had wanted) made what turned out to be a 58 game 2025-26 season with such a small squad an impossible job for Eddie Howe, rather than just very difficult.

Whether it was intentional or not, the shift by the Newcastle United owners in making Ross Wilson the main man then directly led to Eddie Howe leaving. Also ensuring that Bruno Guimaraes was going to be leaving as well.

What happens next at our football club remains to be seen.

As always with Newcastle United I am hoping for the best but fearing the worst.

#1999. West Ham Have Hired A Championship Specialist – And I’m Delighted

A lot has already been written about incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker, and I make absolutely no apologies for being excited about his appointment.

To be crystal clear, Parker probably wouldn’t have been my first choice. But I’d reached the conclusion that Nuno Espírito Santo was incapable of taking West Ham forward, and with the club desperately needing to revive its Championship promotion campaign, a change was essential.

Is Scott Parker capable of doing that? Absolutely. As Claret & Hugh has confirmed through its own sources at West Ham, Parker is set to become the Hammers’ new head coach. And I believe there are two particular qualities that could make him exactly what this team needs.

I understand there are reservations about Parker’s record in the Premier League, and perhaps even the football his Burnley team played during their most recent promotion campaign.

After all, Burnley had the meanest defence in the Championship, and some supporters are understandably concerned that West Ham might be replacing one cautious manager with another.

But far from viewing that defensive record as a negative, I’d suggest West Ham desperately need somebody capable of improving our back line.

We’ve looked disorganised defensively for far too long, and a manager who can actually get players defending properly would be a welcome change.

Espirito Santo could not fix West Ham’s defence

Not that I want us to be boring, of course.

I also believe Parker is capable of getting more out of the players in attack, particularly the likes of Jarrod Bowen, Divine Mukasa and Lewis Orford.

And there’s something else worth remembering.

Parker has achieved promotion from the Championship with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley. Three promotions with three different clubs.

That’s not a bad record for somebody being brought in to do precisely the same job at West Ham.

I’m often reminded of something former Blackburn Rovers manager Mark Hughes said about signing striker Roque Santa Cruz.

Hughes explained that he’d watched the player countless times but decided to concentrate on what he could do rather than obsessing over his flaws.

It’s something that has always stuck in my mind.

And I think it’s particularly relevant when assessing Parker.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on his shortcomings, I’d prefer to focus on two qualities that I believe could make an enormous difference at West Ham.

Parker is an infectious character and a motivational speaker. He’s somebody who communicates with passion and conviction, and I believe that alone could make a considerable difference to this squad.

In short, I think he’s a far better communicator than Nuno Espírito Santo.

That might sound like a relatively small thing, but I don’t believe it is.

West Ham have looked like a team lacking confidence, direction and motivation for much of this season.

A manager who can get his message across clearly and make players believe in what they’re doing could transform performances without changing a single member of the squad.

One of my biggest frustrations with Espírito Santo was his apparent inability to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to football matches.

Time and again, we’d begin games slowly, allow opponents to take control and then spend the rest of the afternoon trying to recover.

It was a problem Nuno repeatedly acknowledged but never seemed capable of fixing.

And I suspect motivation played a significant part in that.

Whatever else people might say about Parker, I find it difficult to imagine his players routinely wandering onto the pitch looking half asleep. He’ll have them fired up, motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle.

Of course, enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to win football matches.

But Parker also has the tactical experience to back it up.

He’s demonstrated that he understands the Championship, knows how to organise a team and can put together a successful promotion campaign.

I certainly don’t expect him to be out-thought tactically by virtually every opposition manager, which increasingly appeared to be the case under Nuno.

And while there will undoubtedly be questions about how Parker’s methods translate to the Premier League, that’s a discussion for another day.

We’re in the Championship, and our immediate priority is getting out of it.

Scott Parker has already demonstrated on three separate occasions that he knows exactly how to do that.

In short, Scotty P understands this Championship stuff considerably better than Nuno ever appeared to.

And I don’t see too much wrong with appointing a specialist for the job.

#1998. “Scot Will Be There” Parker’s First West Ham Decisions Could Come Within Hours

Claret & Hugh has been informed within the past few moments that incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker is likely to have some input into team selection for tomorrow night’s Championship game against Cardiff City. The former Hammers midfielder is also expected to attend the match, despite Mark Noble being set to take charge on the touchline.

As West Ham confirmed in their official statement earlier today, Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville have been placed in temporary charge of preparations following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo. However, the information we’ve received suggests that Parker could still have a say in the team that faces Cardiff.

A C&H source told us just moments ago: “Scot will be there and he’ll have some influence on the team even if he can’t do all of it.”

West Ham’s final training session ahead of the match took place earlier today at Rush Green, before Parker had even signed his proposed two-and-a-half-year contract. But that doesn’t mean he will have no input at all, particularly with the new manager expected to be in attendance tomorrow evening.

Being something of a Championship specialist, and of course a former Hammer, Parker will already be familiar with West Ham’s form and performances this season. I suspect he’ll also have a reasonable idea of which players he wants in the team and which ones might benefit from a spell on the sidelines.

As Claret & Hugh revealed earlier today, Parker’s proposed contract is closely tied to West Ham securing promotion this season. With that in mind, there is every reason for him to want to influence proceedings as quickly as possible, even if Noble is the man officially overseeing tomorrow’s game.

And, to be perfectly honest, I don’t think Parker needs to reinvent the wheel to make some immediate improvements.

There are a couple of really easy wins available to the new Irons gaffer, and some of them should be blindingly obvious to anybody who has watched West Ham over the past few months.

Morato was Nuno’s first choice left back.

Firstly, a rousing team talk and a little bit of urgency might be enough to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to games. It was a recurring problem under Nuno Espírito Santo, and one the former manager never seemed capable of fixing. Getting the players motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle would be a welcome change.

Then there’s the fairly straightforward business of putting round pegs in round holes. For starters, let’s play an actual left-back in the left-back position. That alone would immediately improve the balance of the team rather than continuing to ask players to operate in unfamiliar roles.

Finding the right blend in midfield would also be of huge benefit. West Ham have spent far too much time surrendering control of what is arguably the most important area of the pitch, despite having some talented options available. Getting that balance right could make an enormous difference to the team’s performances.

And finally, there’s Jarrod Bowen. Surely one of the most obvious priorities for any incoming West Ham manager is getting our best attacking player into as many goalscoring positions as possible. Bowen has spent far too much time being asked to produce something out of nothing, and a better-functioning team should make his job considerably easier.

Okay, it’s all a bit paint by numbers, and there’s nothing particularly revolutionary or overly tactical about those suggestions. But that’s rather the point.

West Ham’s problems have often appeared so obvious that you wonder why they’ve been allowed to continue for so long. Parker doesn’t necessarily need weeks on the training ground to recognise them, and even a quick word with the players before kick-off might help address some of the most glaring deficiencies.

Of course, Noble will be responsible for managing the team against Cardiff, and there’s only so much Parker can realistically influence before he’s properly taken charge.

But if the new manager can offer a few sensible suggestions and inject a little urgency into proceedings, I’d suggest that would already be a step in the right direction.
